passages.t: Remember your Creator before the house falls silent
passages.happening:
‘Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come’ (verse 1), before the years come when you will say you find no pleasure in them. Before the sun, moon and stars grow dark and the clouds return after the rain (verse 2).

Then a poem of a great house falling silent. The keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop, the grinders stop because they are few, and those looking through the windows see dimly (verse 3). The doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades; a person wakes at the sound of a bird, and all the songs grow faint (verse 4). People fear heights and the dangers of the road, the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and desire fails, ‘for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets’ (verse 5).

‘Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed, before the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well’ (verse 6), ‘before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it’ (verse 7).

And the Teacher's last words are the book's first: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher. “Everything is futile!” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 11 ended by calling the young to rejoice while knowing God will judge. Chapter 12 goes straight on with the book's most urgent command: remember your Creator. In Hebrew verses 1 to 7 are one long sentence, held together by the word ‘before’.

Since ancient times many readers have heard the poem as a picture of the aging body. The keepers who tremble are the arms and hands, the strong men who stoop are the legs, the grinders who are few are the teeth, those at the windows are the eyes, the almond blossom is white hair, and the grasshopper dragging itself is the stiff walk of old age. Others read it more simply as a household or town falling silent at a death, with mourners in the streets, or as a gathering storm. Many hear both an aging body and a dying house.

Verse 6 pictures things that break: a silver cord holding a golden lamp bowl, a pitcher at a spring, a wheel at a well. Each is a picture of life's supply coming to an end. Verse 7 echoes Genesis, where God formed the man from dust and breathed life into him.

The poem speaks of old age and death with dignity, not dread. It asks the young to remember God now, while life is full.
passages.later: Verse 7 reaches back to the beginning: ‘Then the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils’ (Genesis 2:7). And the psalm asks for the wisdom this poem teaches: ‘So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom’ (Psalm 90:12).
passages.asks: Remember your Creator before the days grow dark. If you are young, ask what it would mean to remember God now, in the days of strength. And if you are older, ask God to let you meet these days with the dignity this poem gives them.

passages.t: The narrator's last word: fear God
passages.happening:
Now a second voice speaks about the Teacher. ‘Not only was the Teacher wise, but he also taught the people knowledge; he pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs’ (verse 9). ‘The Teacher searched to find delightful sayings and to record accurate words of truth’ (verse 10).

‘The words of the wise are like goads, and the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd’ (verse 11). ‘And by these, my son, be further warned: There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body’ (verse 12).

Then the conclusion: “When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man. For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
These verses speak of the Teacher in the third person. The narrator who introduced him in 1:1 steps forward to say how to hear everything that came before, and to speak to the reader as a son, as the father of Proverbs did.

Goads were pointed sticks used to drive oxen, and nails were driven in firmly. The words of the wise both prod and steady. The single Shepherd who gives them is usually taken to be God himself, though some read it as Solomon or as the human teacher who gathered the sayings.

Verse 12 is a dry, kind warning to anyone who studies: books never end, and too much study wears out the body.

The book ends not with an answer to every question the Teacher raised, but with the fear of God and the certainty of his judgment. Nothing hidden will be overlooked.
passages.later: The motto of the book's ending is the motto of Proverbs' beginning: ‘The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge’ (Proverbs 1:7). And Job's poem on wisdom ends in the same place (Job 28:28).
passages.hard:
Does the epilogue contradict the Teacher, or was it added to make a skeptical book acceptable?

Some scholars have argued that the epilogue was added by a later editor to soften a skeptical book and secure its place among the sacred writings. Others, among them Michael V. Fox, have argued that the book was designed from the start as the words of the Teacher framed by a narrator, so that the epilogue belongs to its structure.

Among those who see a frame, some think the narrator gently distances himself from the Teacher's sharpest conclusions. Others think he endorses them, since he calls the Teacher wise and his words accurate and true (verses 9-10).

Still others point out that the fear of God and God's judgment are not new ideas here. The Teacher himself commanded the fear of God (5:7) and warned of judgment (3:17; 11:9). On this reading the conclusion does not overturn the Teacher's search. It names where the search was heading.

How the book was put together is an open question, and these notes take no side. Readers across these views agree that the book as it stands asks to be read with its conclusion.
passages.asks: The whole duty of man is to fear God and keep his commandments. Ask what of the Teacher's questions you are still carrying, and whether you can carry them inside the fear of God. And ask what hidden thing in your life you would want to set right, knowing that God sees it.
